You could say I’ve found myself in a Double Bind. I’m incredibly torn on this. The film is both undoubtedly ahead of its time and deeply of its time. It has a complete and total understanding of fandom and stan culture most contemporary films should be jealous of, before either had even been born let alone matured to what they are now. The psychological examination of Mima is fascinating and the film abandons all tradition when it comes to structure to force its audience into her perspective and feel as though you’re losing your mind along with her. However, in the twisty third act that level of intense scrutiny when it comes to Mima’s psychology is left by the wayside. I’m not a fan of the Rumi twist. When a film is entirely about the inner workings of someone’s mind and then suddenly decides to be about someone else’s sudden mental break I’m just left a little annoyed. It’s not even that it feels like it comes out of nowhere but that it’s so much less interesting. Suddenly the film is about a bitter, older, fatter woman desperately deluding herself as she cloys for the attention a younger, prettier, thinner girl is getting. A played out trope that’s usage here borders on misogynistic? Mima’s struggle isn’t about perfection (which is why the claim Black Swan ripped this movie off beat for best makes no sense to me, clearly took inspiration but the cores are so different) it’s about identity. So the personification of her struggle with identity no longer being a part of her but someone else seems to undermine that journey. Especially, because once Rumi is revealed, the film ends and Mima is perfectly fine and self assured again. I just feel underwhelmed. Something so interesting becomes so dull. It feels like the film is dedicated to trying to tell an earnest story about being a woman in the spotlight and in some places it succeeds but in others it feels like it falls directly in line with what it’s trying to critique. I’m not someone that thinks rape or sexual assault should never be depicted. Artists have a right to create art about anything they want to. These things are real so of course there should be stories about them. And while the sexual assault and rape scenes (whether real ir acted) are intentionally disturbing in an affective way, they also seem to be drawn and directed in such a way to titillate the viewer. Now, I understand that this is a film about voyeurism and it’s absolutely drenched in metaphor. I don’t think this is just some misogynistic torture porn it’s not that simple. I think it tries to be a story exposing the horrific reality many women face, whether that be the threat of sexual violence or being pressured and pushed into uncomfortable situations or society’s crazymaking obsession with youth and fame and attention being forced upon them. I think in some places it succeeds and in some places it fails. Part of me thinks a big reason why this has the reputation it does is because it’s an anime and if this same film were made in live action there would be less fondness for it. And I mean it is a very well animated film although not much differentiates it from most anime I’ve seen on a technical level. On a thematic level I think everything here is pushing towards a cohesive whole. Every element has something to do with fame and audience and compromise and voyeurism and obsession. There is a thematic throughline here that is definite. But that seems to come at the expense of a throughline for our narrative and characters. Which I’m often more than happy to look past but here so much of this film is built around character. It’s almost a character study of Mima for most of its runtime. So to have that element become so muddled is a real shame. I did really enjoy my time with this. It’s so disorienting and thrilling but I struggle to look past how disappointed I was with the ending, and it’s half baked condemnation of misogyny and rape culture.

This is an incredible film, one that at first made me wonder why it was animated to begin with, but quickly became a showcase for it. The themes of identity are easier to present in this medium, with some brilliant shots to convey that, and I also find it intriguing to consider how it moves us out of reality so we question hers more. This is a very dense movie, and there’s no way I could cover it all, so I’ll simply say that I appreciate its efforts to respect those with a mental illness (usually this particular kind of plot will have me rolling my eyes too much to actually latch onto it outside of academically — see also: Psycho ) while still being damned entertaining. It’s a horror concept that is made so by caring about the people it’s happening to; it’s scary for the character, not just those around the character or those watching at home (see also: Split ). Well done balancing act which makes horror out of compassion, and those things are so oft linked in real life and so rarely explored together in film. There’s a sequence here where the protagonist is waking up from a dream within a dream repeatedly, and it fooled me every single time. That scene brought me to the edge of my seat with my hand covering my mouth out of suspense. I think this is one of the best foreign language films I’ve ever seen. Best Thing: The story. Even more impressive than the sometimes jaw-dropping animation, I loved the story. It’s gripping, and it’s powerful, and I certainly did not call the twist. Worst Thing: [ crickets ] Watched Subbed.

A beautiful, astonishingly well-written exploration of the objectification of pop stars, the paranoia inherent to being a celebrity and being surrounded by potential enemies at all times, the psychological effects of being a woman and being surrounded by larger men who would be more than happy to rape you if the opportunity presented itself, the difference between our professional and personal personas and the troubles that can arise if those boundaries blur, and the jealousy older women have for younger women once their sexual value has subsided, all of it set at the dawn of the Internet (which has turned us all into mini-celebrities to some degree). I must confess at the outset that one of my big life goals is to become a pornographer. I've never wanted children, and after a few lucrative decades spent training for and then succeeding at high-paying Silicon Valley tech jobs, I am restless to spend my thirties becoming physically strong and sexually virile. I want to become extremely strong and create an OnlyFans where I make love to a succession of beautiful, ideally white, young women in both conventional and comedic scenarios, filmed POV. There's not much profit in it, but frankly, I already have enough money (for myself to live off, so don't get any bright ideas that I'm Richie Rich). The whole point of making money is to ultimately be able to do what you want with your life. Some men want to race cars, others to raise large families, others to hunt and fish. I want to direct adult films and be a stud. (I also have higher-minded, more conventional artistic goals as relates to my own people, the Hindus, but those might be more of a later-life thing. I have time.) I tell you this to make it clear that I'm not approaching Perfect Blue from a feminist angle. My view is that all of life, from the smallest bacterium to the blue whale, is an abattoir where the strong feast upon the weak. While fossil fuels allowed us a brief reprieve from Malthusian brutality for a short few centuries, our population has increased, our technology has stagnated, and our climate is changing to the point that the "law of the jungle" is once again taking hold. I view Perfect Blue as a chronicle of the return of Japanese civilization (and all civilization more broadly) to something more primal as humanity leaves our peak years behind us. My expectation is that humans in 2200 will envy the lifestyles of peasants in 1200. Mima is a pop idol trying to transition into becoming an actress. As an idol, she mostly performed for horny middle-aged men and local louts, and she hopes for a more dignified career as she ages. Ironically, her background and the changing times get her cast in "degrading" roles, and her breakout role is playing a stripper who gets raped by the crowd. (Don't mind that scribbling you hear in the background, I'm just taking notes for my own work.) She also strips for various photoshoots (to my pleasure, said shots show her vulva - director Satoshi Kon doesn't pussy out in the way Western directors would). Throughout the film, we're treated to various shots showing murders and such, only to then hear a director yelling "Cut!" and realize that it was just shots from her acting career. So when actors and directors associated with Mima start turning up dead and an ugly stalker obsessed with Mima arrives without any cameras around, we start to realize that Mima is in actual danger. Figuring out what's real and what isn't is most of the fun of the film's incredible plotting, and while I personally didn't like the happy ending and twist culprit (I think it would have been more interesting to see Mima raped and killed by a deranged stalker, frankly), I understand that normal audiences would not be okay with that, and poor Mr. Kon probably wouldn't be invited to direct more high-budget films. My personal ending is that the film fades to black as the stalker assaults Mima. I watched Perfect Blue in the theater on a lark when I happened to come across its listing on Fandango (I watched Paprika by Kon years ago and was not impressed, so it's unlikely I would have watched this on my own without the prod from the theater).
